title: AQA English Language Paper 2 Question 5: Viewpoint Writing (2026 Format)
description: How to answer AQA Paper 2 Question 5 in 2026: build a convincing argument, adapt to audience and form, structure ideas and secure the 24/16 mark split.

children: Paper 2 Question 5 is worth 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). The task asks you to communicate a viewpoint for a specified audience, purpose and form. From 2026, AQA’s mark scheme includes clearer examples of the typical features seen at different levels, including the quality of argument, register, sequencing, rhetorical crafting and control of tone.
Argument first; devices second

A persuasive-device checklist does not create a convincing response by itself. The strongest writing has a developed line of thought, adapts to the audience and uses rhetoric to sharpen ideas. Decide what you actually believe—or what position you can argue convincingly—before choosing techniques.
A five-stage plan
Define your position in one sentence. Avoid a vague “there are pros and cons” unless the task genuinely calls for balance.
Identify the audience. What assumptions, concerns or priorities are likely to matter to them?
Plan three developed ideas that move the argument forward rather than repeating the same claim.
Include at least one point of complication or counterargument so the writing feels considered rather than simplistic.
Choose an ending that changes pressure: a clear call, warning, challenge, proposal or final image.
Make the form visible without parodying it
A speech should sound speakable and aware of listeners.
An article needs a controlled public voice and clear organisation.
A letter should establish an appropriate relationship with its recipient.
A leaflet or guide needs clarity and purposeful organisation.
Whatever the form, do not waste half a page on decorative headings if the actual argument remains thin.
Rhetorical methods that earn their place

Rhetorical questions, direct address, repetition, contrast, anecdote, statistics, tricolon and figurative language can all be useful. The test is simple: does the choice strengthen this idea for this audience? If you could paste the sentence into any persuasive task, it may be too generic.
Mini-example: develop rather than list

Weak: “Public transport is cheaper, greener and better. Do you really want pollution?” Stronger: start with a concrete tension—people may agree that fewer car journeys would help towns, while still needing reliable transport for work or caring responsibilities. That gives you something to argue: change succeeds only when the alternative is genuinely usable. Rhetoric can then develop the reasoning rather than replace it.
Control tone across the response
Vary intensity. Constant outrage quickly becomes monotonous.
Use concessions strategically: acknowledging a sensible opposing point can make your own position more credible.
Move between example and principle so the argument has both detail and scale.
Return to key language or an image to create cohesion.
Use paragraph openings to signal development, not just “Firstly, secondly, thirdly”.
AO6: protect the 16 marks

Technical accuracy includes sentence control, punctuation, spelling and vocabulary. Ambition helps only when it remains accurate. Build a proofreading routine around your known errors rather than scanning vaguely at the end.
Common mistakes
Writing a list of rhetorical devices with no developed argument.
Forgetting the stated audience or form after the opening.
Repeating the same reason in slightly different language.
Inventing implausible statistics and presenting them as facts.
Using sentence fragments or punctuation for “effect” without controlling the grammar.
Final checklist
My viewpoint is clear and developed.
My ideas progress rather than repeat.
Tone and register fit the audience and form.
Rhetorical choices strengthen specific ideas.
I have checked sentence boundaries, spelling and punctuation.
